sections.title: The Ray Aspect of Light
objectives: List the ways by which light travels from a source to another location.
Explain the ray model of light and when it is a good approximation.

misconceptions.claim: A ray bends towards the normal when it enters glass from air.
misconceptions.correction: It bends away from the normal, because the speed of light is lower in glass.

summary: A straight line that originates at some point is called a ray.
The part of optics dealing with the ray aspect of light is called geometric optics.
Light can travel in three ways from a source to another location: (1) directly from the source through empty space; (2) through various media; (3) after being reflected from a mirror.

authored_exercises.answer: A straight line drawn in the direction in which light energy travels.
solution: Light spreads out from a source.
In the ray model we represent its direction of travel by a line.
The line is perpendicular to the wavefronts.

authored_exercises.stem: Name two ways light can travel from a source to a place where it is seen.
authored_exercises.answer: Directly through a vacuum or air, or after reflection and refraction by surfaces along the way.
solution: Light can travel straight from the source to the eye.
It can also reflect from a mirror or diffuse surface.
It can refract through glass, water or the lens of the eye.

sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source section on The Ray Aspect of Light has no worked example; the teaching text derives the key results and the practice set applies them.

sections.title: The Law of Reflection
objectives: Explain reflection of light from polished and rough surfaces.
State the law of reflection and apply it to plane and curved mirrors.
Distinguish specular reflection from diffuse reflection.

misconceptions.claim: The law of reflection says the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, both measured from the surface.
misconceptions.correction: Both angles are measured from the normal, the line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence. Measuring from the surface gives a different pair of numbers, though the two are complementary.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-3, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question asks which angle the reflection angle equals.

summary: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.
A mirror has a smooth surface and reflects light at specific angles.
Light is diffused when it reflects from a rough surface.

authored_exercises.answer: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal all lie in the same plane.
solution: Angles are measured from the normal, not the surface.
The reflected ray leaves on the opposite side of the normal.
Both rays and the normal lie in one plane.

authored_exercises.stem: Why can you see your face in a mirror but not in a sheet of white paper?
authored_exercises.answer: The mirror reflects light specularly in one direction, while the paper reflects diffusely in many directions.
solution: A smooth surface reflects a parallel beam as a parallel beam.
A rough surface scatters the light in many directions.
Only the specular reflection preserves the image.

authored_exercises.stem: A ray strikes a plane mirror at 35° to the normal. What is the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray?
solution: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, 35°.
The incident and reflected rays lie on opposite sides of the normal.
The angle between them is 35° + 35° = 70°.

sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source section on The Law of Reflection has no worked example; the teaching text derives the key results and the practice set applies them.

sections.title: The Law of Refraction
objectives: Determine the index of refraction, given the speed of light in a medium.
State Snell’s law and calculate the angle of refraction at a boundary.

misconceptions.claim: A converging lens forms an image at the same place whatever the object distance.
misconceptions.correction: The image distance changes with the object distance, and the lens equation gives it.

misconceptions.claim: Snell's law relates the angles of incidence and refraction to the wavelengths in the two media.
misconceptions.correction: It relates them to the speeds of light, through the refractive indices. The wavelengths change as the speed changes, and the frequency does not, which is the point of the law.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-4, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the wavelength reading as an option.

summary: The changing of a light ray’s direction when it passes through variations in matter is called refraction.
The speed of light in vacuum c=2.99792458×108 m/s≈3.00×108 m/s.
Index of refraction n=cv, where v is the speed of light in the material, c is the speed of light in vacuum, and n is the index of refraction.

sections.title: Total Internal Reflection
objectives: Explain the phenomenon of total internal reflection.
Describe the workings and uses of fiber optics.
Analyze the reason for the sparkle of diamonds.

misconceptions.claim: Total internal reflection can occur when light travels from air into glass.
misconceptions.correction: It can occur only when light travels from a denser medium into a less dense one and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle. Going from air to glass bends the ray toward the normal instead.

misconceptions.claim: An optical fibre keeps light inside because its cladding is opaque.
misconceptions.correction: The core has a higher refractive index than the cladding. Light striking the boundary above the critical angle undergoes total internal reflection, so it stays in the core.

summary: The incident angle that produces an angle of refraction of 90º is called critical angle.

Total internal reflection is a phenomenon that occurs at the boundary between two mediums, such that if the incident angle in the first medium is greater than the critical angle, then all the light is reflected back into that medium.
Fiber optics involves the transmission of light down fibers of plastic or glass, applying the principle of total internal reflection.

authored_exercises.answer: The angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction is 90°.
solution: Light bends away from the normal when it enters a less dense medium.
At the critical angle the refracted ray grazes the boundary.
Beyond it, total internal reflection occurs.

authored_exercises.stem: A diver shines a flashlight beam upward from beneath the water surface. The index of refraction of water is 1.33 and that of air is 1.00. (a) Calculate the critical angle for the water-air boundary. (b) Can the light escape into the air if the beam strikes the surface at 60° from the normal? Explain.
authored_exercises.answer: (a) 48.8° (b) No: 60° exceeds the critical angle, so the light is totally internally reflected back into the water
solution: Snell's law at the critical angle: n_water sin θc = n_air sin 90°, so sin θc = 1.00/1.33 = 0.752.
The angle of incidence 60° is larger than 48.8°, so Snell's law gives no refracted ray: the light is totally internally reflected and cannot escape.

sections.title: Dispersion: The Rainbow and Prisms
objectives: Explain the phenomenon of dispersion and discuss its advantages and disadvantages.
Explain how dispersion separates white light into colours, and how a rainbow forms.

misconceptions.claim: A prism bends all colours of white light by the same angle.
misconceptions.correction: The refractive index depends on wavelength. Violet light is refracted more than red light, so the colours leave the prism at different angles and the light is dispersed.

summary: The spreading of white light into its full spectrum of wavelengths is called dispersion.
Rainbows are produced by a combination of refraction and reflection and involve the dispersion of sunlight into a continuous distribution of colors.
Dispersion produces beautiful rainbows but also causes problems in certain optical systems.

authored_exercises.stem: A narrow beam of white light in air strikes one face of a 60.0° crown-glass prism at 45.0° incidence. Crown glass has n = 1.512 for red light and n = 1.530 for violet light. (a) Use Snell's law at both surfaces to calculate the deviation of each colour. (b) Which colour is deviated more, and why does the white light spread into a spectrum?
authored_exercises.answer: (a) The red ray deviates by 38.5° and the violet ray by 40.3° (b) Violet, because its larger index bends it more at both surfaces; the spread of deviations fans the colours out into a spectrum
solution: First surface, red: sin r = sin 45.0°/1.512, r = 27.9°. Second surface: incidence = 60.0° - 27.9° = 32.1°, sin i' = 1.512 × sin 32.1°, i' = 53.5°.
Violet is deviated about 1.8° more than red, so the colours leave the prism at slightly different angles and form a spectrum.

sections.title: Image Formation by Lenses
objectives: List the rules for ray tracing for thin lenses.
Illustrate the formation of images using the technique of ray tracing.
Determine power of a lens given the focal length.

misconceptions.claim: A convex lens always forms a real image.
misconceptions.correction: When the object is closer than the focal length, a convex lens forms a virtual, upright, magnified image. A real image forms only when the object is beyond the focal point.

summary: Light rays entering a converging lens parallel to its axis cross one another at a single point on the opposite side.
For a converging lens, the focal point is the point at which converging light rays cross; for a diverging lens, the focal point is the point from which diverging light rays appear to originate.
The distance from the center of the lens to its focal point is called the focal length f.

sections.title: Image Formation by Mirrors
objectives: Illustrate image formation in a flat mirror.
Explain with ray diagrams the formation of an image using spherical mirrors.
Determine focal length and magnification given radius of curvature, distance of object and image.

misconceptions.claim: A plane mirror reverses left and right.
misconceptions.correction: A plane mirror reverses front and back. The image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, and it has the same size and orientation.

summary: The characteristics of an image formed by a flat mirror are: (a) The image and object are the same distance from the mirror, (b) The image is a virtual image, and (c) The image is situated behind the mirror.
Image length is half the radius of curvature. f=R2
A convex mirror is a diverging mirror and forms only one type of image, namely a virtual image.

sec-2:exr-15.stem: Suppose a man stands in front of a mirror. His eyes are 1.65 m above the floor, and the top of his head is 0.13 m higher. Find the height above the floor of the top and bottom of the smallest mirror in which he can see both the top of his head and his feet. How is this distance related to the man’s height?

sec-7:exr-148.stem: A book held 7.50 cm from a 10.0 cm focal length magnifying glass has a magnification of 4.00. (a) Find the magnification for the book when it is held 8.50 cm from the magnifier. (b) Do the same for when it is held 9.50 cm from the magnifier. (c) Comment on the trend in m as the object distance increases as in these two calculations.

sec-4:exr-85.stem: What is the speed of light in water? In glycerine? Take the index of refraction of water as 1.333 and that of glycerine as 1.473.
sec-4:exr-85.solution_provenance: OpenStax CNXML solution element (in file); the source answer gave only the glycerine speed

sec-4:exr-91.stem: Calculate the index of refraction for a medium in which the speed of light is $2.012\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s}$, and identify the most likely substance using these values: water 1.333, ethanol 1.361, fused quartz 1.458, polystyrene 1.490, crown glass 1.52, flint glass 1.66, diamond 2.419.
solution: The index of refraction is $n=c/v=(3.00\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s})/(2.012\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s})=1.491$.
The closest tabulated value is 1.490, so the medium is polystyrene.

steps: The index of refraction is $n=c/v$, so $v=c/n$ .
This is slightly more than half the speed of light in vacuum, and still very fast by everyday standards.
Diamond has a larger index of refraction than zircon, so light travels even more slowly in diamond; this is why zircon sparkles less than diamond.

sec-4:we-ex-29.statement: Determine the Index of Refraction from Refraction Data
steps: Medium 1 is air with $n_{1}=1.00$; the incident angle is $θ_{1}=30.0°$ and the angle of refraction is $θ_{2}=22.0°$ .
Snell's law gives $n_{1}\\sinθ_{1}=n_{2}\\sinθ_{2}$ .
This is the index of refraction of water.
Light goes from air ($n_{1}=1.00$) into diamond ($n_{2}=2.419$) at $θ_{1}=30.0°$ .
Snell's law gives $n_{1}\\sinθ_{1}=n_{2}\\sinθ_{2}$ .
$θ_{2}=11.9°$, much smaller than the $22.0°$ obtained for water at the same incident angle.

sec-5:we-ex-10.statement: How Big is the Critical Angle Here?
steps: For light in polystyrene ($n_{1}=1.49$) surrounded by air ($n_{2}=1.00$), the critical angle is given by $\\sinθ_{c}=n_{2}/n_{1}$ .
Any ray inside the plastic striking the surface at more than $42.2°$ is totally internally reflected.

sec-7:we-ex-12.statement: What is the Power of a Common Magnifying Glass?
steps: The Sun is so far away that its rays are parallel when they reach the lens, so the lens focuses them at its focal point.
The distance from the lens to the bright spot is the focal length: $f=8.00cm=0.0800m$ .
The power of a lens is $P=1/f$ .

sec-7:we-ex-41.statement: Finding the Image of a Light Bulb Filament by Ray Tracing and by the Thin Lens Equations
sec-7:we-ex-41.answer: $d_{i}=1.50m$, $m=-2.00$ (a real, inverted image twice the object's size)
steps: The object is $d_{o}=0.750m$ from a convex lens of focal length $f=0.500m$ .
The thin lens equation gives $1/d_{i}=1/f-1/d_{o}=1/0.500-1/0.750$ .
The magnification is $m=-d_{i}/d_{o}=-1.50/0.750=-2.00$ .
The image is real (positive $d_{i}$), inverted (negative $m$), and twice the size of the object, in agreement with the ray-tracing construction.

sec-7:we-ex-63.statement: Image Produced by a Magnifying Glass
steps: The object is $d_{o}=7.50cm$ from a convex lens of focal length $f=10.0cm$, so it lies inside the focal point.
$d_{i}=-30.0cm$; the negative sign means the image is virtual and on the same side as the object.
The image is upright and four times the size of the object.

sec-7:we-ex-75.statement: Image Produced by a Concave Lens
steps: The object is $d_{o}=7.50cm$ from a concave lens of focal length $f=-10.0cm$ .
$d_{i}=-4.29cm$; the image is virtual and on the same side as the object.
The image is upright and a little over half the object's size.
The mirror has radius of curvature $R=50.0cm$, so its focal length is $f=R/2=25.0cm=0.250m$ .
The image is real and $d_{i}=3.00m$ from the mirror.
The mirror equation gives $1/d_{o}=1/f-1/d_{i}=1/0.250-1/3.00$ .
The coils sit only slightly beyond the focal point, and the image is far away, as in a slide projector.

sec-8:we-ex-40.answer: radius of curvature about 0.79 cm (focal length about -0.40 cm)
steps: The cornea acts as a convex mirror. The object is $d_{o}=12.0cm$ away and the magnification is $m=0.0320$ .
The mirror equation gives $1/f=1/d_{o}+1/d_{i}=1/12.0+1/(-0.384)$ .
The radius of curvature is $R=2f=-0.793cm$; its magnitude is about 0.79 cm.
